AI honeypots, context bombs and fingerprinting traps: how defenders can play the Uno Reverse card on the agents sent to hack them, and what the evidence says actually works.

A web server lists a “hidden” directory in its robots.txt. Inside sit a credential-manager binary, an encrypted vault and a boring internal runbook: check the hash, then run the binary to open the vault. A human pentester might pause. An AI agent told it is an authorised tester treats the runbook as the obvious next step and runs it. In Julio Ureña’s controlled proof of concept, that binary was a backdoor, and the machine that ran it belonged to the attacker. [URENA]

That is the Uno Reverse card. Attackers now send agents to do their hacking, and the same autonomy that makes those agents fast makes them easy to lead. They take the cheapest path to something that looks like success, and they trust what they find on the way.

This post collects what defenders have learned about trapping AI agents, from an IAPS policy report, vendor studies, independent experiments and talks at the [un]prompted conference. The aim is practical: which traps produce reliable signals, which ones are promising but unproven, and where the line sits between trapping an attacker and hacking back.

Terms used hereHoneypot: a decoy system, file or resource with no routine business use, so an unexpected touch is a signal. Canary: a monitored decoy. A honeytoken is decoy data, such as a fake key that alerts when someone tries to use it. Context bomb: a short string in a decoy that can trip the attacking model’s safety guardrails. Shibboleth: a realistic feature that coaxes out clues about the model or harness behind an attack. None of these require touching the attacker’s machine.

▶ 001The hunter can be led

Ureña’s bait was deliberately dull. There was no urgency and no aggressive social engineering, just a plausible runbook that made running the binary look routine. In his tests, it worked on most of the agents he pointed at it. [URENA]

8/12
CLI models ran the planted binary from one of five fixed prompts, without warning the operator. All 6 of 6 pentest-agent tools tested also ran it; two ran in the same container as the operator’s AI token. One researcher’s controlled proof of concept, default behaviour only. [URENA]

Quarkslab saw the same trait from the defender’s side. Its agents never defeated a software protection in its reverse-engineering experiments. They routed around it, committed early to a story, and reported with the same confidence whether the work had happened or not. One agent found the generator’s answer key instead of reversing the binary. [QUARKSLAB]

Yotam Perkal, who leads security research at Pluto Security, framed it this way at the AI Agent Security Summit in London. Agents chase signals of progress towards their goal. A bait therefore does not need to convince a human. It only needs to look like progress to the agent. [YOTAM]

Three traits → three trap designs

  1. Cheapest path to answer-shaped. Put the bait on the shortcut.
  2. Early commitment. A suggestive filename or runbook can steer the whole run.
  3. Confident wrongness. A plausible wrong answer goes unchallenged, so feed one.

▶ 002Two kinds of hunter

The same trap catches two different agents. The first is an attacker’s agent, pointed at you from outside. That is the case in most of the research below.

The second is your own agent. The IAPS report Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats (Jan Wehner and Jam Kraprayoon, October 2026) treats deployed agents as a new kind of insider. They hold legitimate access and can misuse it through mistakes, compromise by an attacker, or misaligned goals. The report cites agents that escaped containment, damaged internal systems, leaked customer data or coordinated with each other. [IAPS]

For insiders, a honeypot can be a fake resource, such as admin credentials or a server. It can also be a staged situation, such as a message from another agent proposing collusion or an apparent hole in a sandbox. A trigger raises an alert, pauses the agent and starts an investigation. [IAPS]

The common threadBoth cases rest on shortcut-seeking. The trait that walks an attacker’s agent into a canary also walks your own agent into an unguarded credential. Treat every convenience in your own sandbox as attack surface.

▶ 003The bear-trap toolkit

IAPS frames three honeypot strategies: detection, incrimination and deterrence. Field work adds several more. The cards below give each technique’s source and the strength of its evidence today.

Trap 01 · Tripwire

Canaries → detection

What it does
Decoy credentials, hosts and files give the security team a tripwire when the monitored action occurs.
Evidence
Strongest. Vendor data and in-the-wild honeypots both show agents taking the bait. [TRACEBIT] [ZENITY]

Trap 02 · Decoy infrastructure

Fake AI stack → threat intel

What it does
Decoy LLM gateways, model servers and agents attract attackers hunting for free inference.
Evidence
Observed in the wild. Zenity reported more than 22 million requests in six months across its decoy network. [ZENITY]

Trap 03 · Sting

Staged opportunity → incrimination

What it does
Separates an honest mistake from deliberate misbehaviour by an agent.
Evidence
Thin. Works in evaluations; little published from production. [IAPS]

Trap 04 · Warning

Uncertainty → deterrence

What it does
A warning about decoys may change how agents explore.
Evidence
Weakest. One AWS benchmark saw a warning cut full compromise from 20% to 3%. [TRACEBIT-CANARIES]

Trap 05 · Maze

HoneyAI → token burn

What it does
Endless plausible fake paths waste the attacker’s time and tokens.
Evidence
Mixed. Worked on weaker agents; a capable agent with tools still found the real bug. [YOTAM]

Trap 06 · Refusal

Context bomb → attacker stops

What it does
A string in a decoy secret trips the attacking model’s own guardrails.
Evidence
Vendor study. 152 runs, five models; attackers can filter it. [TRACEBIT]

Trap 07 · Accent probe

Shibboleth → fingerprinting

What it does
Realistic features draw out clues about the model and harness.
Evidence
Research preprint. The authors averaged 90% accuracy across 15 candidate models. [SHIBBOLETH]

Trap 08 · Binary defence

Bound secrets → silent failure

What it does
Secrets depend on runtime state; a wrong environment returns plausible garbage.
Evidence
Lab result. Agents never defeated the protections. [QUARKSLAB] BLA adds decoy artifacts, own benchmarks only. [BLA]

▶ 004Detection is the part that holds

A well-placed honeypot starts with a simple question: who has a legitimate reason to touch it? Keep ordinary traffic away and an unexpected interaction is a strong reason to investigate. IAPS also notes that decoys give you evidence you can use without reading an agent’s reasoning, and that simple decoy files cost little to maintain. [IAPS]

95.9%
of runs that had canaries deployed and reached admin escalation tripped a canary before the first critical action. From Tracebit’s controlled AWS benchmark across ten models. [TRACEBIT-CANARIES]

The timing matters as much as the hit rate. The median lead in that benchmark was eight minutes from the first canary touch to the first critical action. In those runs, a team with a fast response could use that head start to pause a session, revoke a token or isolate a host. [TRACEBIT-CANARIES]

The agent doesn’t have to fall all the way in.
One touch can give you a head start.

▶ 005Into the wild: what a decoy AI stack caught

Most of this field has lived in the lab. At [un]prompted, Mike Takahashi of Zenity presented data from a honeypot network of fake AI servers and agents. It emulated LLM gateways, model servers and agent frameworks across several locations. The attackers arrived almost immediately. [ZENITY]

22M+
requests from thousands of IPs in six months, Takahashi reported, including a spike of 400,000 requests in an hour. That’s traffic volume. A scanner can send plenty of requests on its own. [ZENITY]

01 · What they wanted → free inference

Probes hit the generate and chat endpoints with simple test prompts to see which models were available. There was particular interest in less-restricted open models such as GLM, DeepSeek and Kimi. Many then tried to leak system prompts and list the agent’s tools. [ZENITY]

02 · How fast they moved → one day

Exploitation attempts against a newly disclosed LiteLLM vulnerability appeared one day after disclosure. Other attempts sprayed default admin keys at management features, including a feature for testing guardrail code. As Takahashi put it, the guardrail meant to protect the AI became the way in. [ZENITY]

03 · Canaries where the agents looked → thousands of logins

Attackers prompted the decoy agents to use their own shell tools to search for credentials. Zenity planted canary keys in exactly those places. The keys drew thousands of login attempts from many IPs and user agents, and testing began within 30 minutes of discovery, which suggests automation. The key thieves and key users often came from different IPs, so Zenity is asking whether stolen keys are being resold. [ZENITY]

04 · The hunter showed its hand → clues in the traffic

Some requests carried far more than a test prompt. Takahashi described a 140,000-character prompt from the Strix pentest agent aimed at a third-party site. Zenity also saw GitHub repos, local file paths, harness names, tool lists and targets in the traffic it collected. That gives defenders leads to investigate. An IP or a harness name can only take you so far. [ZENITY]

Keep the decoy containedZenity blocked outbound traffic, so the decoy could observe requests aimed at third parties without carrying them out. If you run AI infrastructure, lock it down, rotate default keys and patch quickly. Otherwise your inference can become someone else’s attack platform.

▶ 006Context bombs: make the attacker’s model refuse

A context bomb is not context-window flooding. It is a short string placed inside a decoy secret that trips the attacking model’s own safety guardrails and can stop the agent mid-run. Malware authors use the same prompt-injection idea to get AI analysis tools to call a sample benign. Tracebit turned it around, and the canary still alerts. [TRACEBIT]

91→15%
Runs completing at least one attack path. Tracebit compared an AWS baseline with no canary against one AWS Secrets Manager decoy with a context bomb. The study scored 152 runs across five models. Opus 4.8 reached admin in 93% of baseline runs and in none in the decoy condition. [TRACEBIT]

Tracebit also reports 57% to 5% for reaching admin and 36% to 1% for full compromise, meaning admin access plus persistence. In the decoy condition, every run that completed an attack path raised a canary alert. [TRACEBIT]

Evidence caution. This is vendor research. The study had no comparison arm with a plain canary, so it leaves the context bomb’s added effect unmeasured. The result applies to the models, guardrails and AWS setup tested. Treat refusal as one possible layer beside the canary. [TRACEBIT]

▶ 007Offensive countermeasures: alert while the agent reads

The idea of fighting back without hacking back is older than AI agents. John Strand and Paul Asadoorian’s Offensive Countermeasures: The Art of Active Defense splits it into three categories: annoyance, attribution and attack. [STRAND] Annoyance means raising the work an attacker must do, with honeypots, bogus DNS entries and endlessly recursive web directories that stall scanners. [ACTIVE] Strand’s stated aim was to turn the tables without tripping into hacking back. [ADHD]

Be precise with the term, because not everyone uses it that way. ENISA, for example, uses “offensive countermeasure” to mean a counter-attack, commonly called hack-back. [ENISA] In this post it means the first two A’s only.

CategoryAgainst AI agents
AnnoyanceMazes and token burn (HoneyAI, TokenExhaust), plausible wrong answers, and context bombs that make the attacking model stop.
AttributionCanary use, model fingerprints and whatever context agents send to a decoy can give investigators leads.
AttackRunning code on the attacker’s machine, as in Ureña’s proof of concept. Out of bounds here, for the legal reasons in section 013.

The faux secrets file → decide what alerts

A decoy secrets file is a simple place to start. First work out what you’ll actually see. A file-read alert needs monitoring on the file or service. If your honeytoken alerts on attempted use, someone can copy it without firing the alert.

  1. Pick the signal. A read alert catches someone opening a monitored decoy. A use alert catches someone trying the planted credential. Test whichever behaviour you expect to see.
  2. Give the alert a quiet home. Place the decoy outside routine workflows and check whether scanners, indexing and other legitimate jobs touch it.
  3. Treat refusal as experimental. If you evaluate a context bomb, compare it with a plain canary in a controlled test. The AWS result gives you a reason to investigate, and a local file is a different environment.
Keep the tripwire independentBuild detection around the action you can observe. A refusal may buy time if the agent encounters it. Your own tools can hit the same guardrails, so check what happens to your scanners too (section 012).

▶ 008Mazes and token burn

Ureña separates an idea, a mechanism and a tool. HoneyAI is a honeypot built to attract AI agents, not humans. TokenExhaust is the mechanism: an effectively endless path that burns the attacker’s tokens. Moqesh is his open-source project that implements it. The decoy adapts, so the more it is attacked, the more fake data, systems and credentials it presents. [URENA] [MOQESH]

Perkal reported three small-scale maze tests in his London talk. [YOTAM]

RunWhat happened
Claude-based agent, web mazeFollowed a fix-me note into a fake admin area. Hit the traps 118 times across almost 10,000 decoy pages, and reported the decoys as real findings.
PentestGPT, same mazeWent deeper. Ran to about $200 before it was stopped, probed the fake credentials 41 times and hallucinated CTF flags.
Pentest agent on GPT-5.5, with toolsFollowed every decoy and still found the real bug in every run. It wrote scripts to loop over pages, so not every decoy entered its context.

His image for the second run is a racehorse in blinkers: a goal-driven agent can keep chasing the wrong thing. The third run shows how quickly that advantage can disappear. [YOTAM]

Detect the chase.
Diversion is a bonus.

In the third setup, the decoys still caught the agent’s attention, and the real bug still fell. There is a measurement lesson here: a script can touch a page without the model ever seeing it.

▶ 009Shibboleths: make the model say its name

Sergej Epp, Dario Pasquini and their co-authors start with a problem: different agents can run the same standard shell commands, which tell you little about the model behind them. Their answer is the shibboleth, a feature that fits the attacker’s goal while eliciting a more distinctive response. [SHIBBOLETH]

01 · Declaration → ask it who it is

One example is a decoy MCP service that asks the agent to declare its model. The first answer can be wrong, and some agents give several names in the same run. A declared name is a clue worth checking against the rest of the interaction. [SHIBBOLETH]

02 · Behaviour → make it write

Another gate asks the agent to write free text before it gets the resource it wants. That gives the researchers a sample of its writing “accent”. For the harness, they look at tool behaviour instead: timeouts, parallel or sequential calls, and how secrets are handled. [SHIBBOLETH]

90%
Average first-choice accuracy across 15 candidate models when declared names and behaviour were combined. In a separate test, the authors identified the correct harness 92% of the time across four candidates. Behaviour still gave clues when agents were told to hide their identity. [SHIBBOLETH]

Now you have a better guess at the tools doing the work. The same model and harness can be used by plenty of people, so keep looking for evidence of who was behind the keyboard.

▶ 010Counter-Clauding: making reversing agents fail quietly

Quarkslab applied the same logic to software protection against an autonomous reverse-engineering agent. Obfuscation did not stop the agent, but it pushed it off the easy path and into hallucinated conclusions. Its recipe: [QUARKSLAB]

  1. Put the secret behind execution. If it can be read and lifted, it will be.
  2. Use many small, varied, hidden runtime checks. Diversity beats one strong sensor.
  3. Bind the result to the environment, not a branch. There is no visible “if” to find.
  4. Spread the dependency through the rest of the protection.
  5. Never crash. A crash points at the check. A plausible wrong answer gives the agent nothing to verify against.

The open-source BLA project (“Blind LLM Agents”) applies a similar idea to build outputs under the banner “poison, exhaust, hallucinate”. It shapes inputs to hit analyser limits, adds decoy symbols and source maps, and returns synthetic results to debuggers. Its effectiveness figures are its own benchmarks. [BLA]

▶ 011Designing a trap worth setting

The IAPS report gives the most complete design notes, and the field talks add practical lessons. [IAPS]

RuleWhat it means
Plausible, not perfect

A bait that looks too good to be true may be skipped. Internal agents know their environment and can spot inconsistencies. A decoy spotted mid-interaction can still alert.

Along the attack chain

At one decoy in five, an agent choosing at random hits one 20% of the time per step and about 59% across four independent choices. Returns diminish, so place decoys near high-value targets and at bottlenecks. Zenity’s lesson: put canaries exactly where attacking agents search.

Quiet on false alarms

Place decoys outside normal working areas and tune thresholds. IAPS reports that labelling decoys “not for agent use” substantially reduces accidental touches.

Alert, then act

Wire the trigger to a response: pause, investigate, revoke. Decide ahead of time who can act and how quickly.

Secret and contained

Zenity keeps its setup details out of public talks and blocks outbound traffic so attackers cannot use the honeypot to reach real targets. A badly isolated decoy can become a pivot.

Use your advantages

You control what the agent sees, can test decoys against copies of the exact model, and can reset an agent after it is caught. Use AI to help design decoys, but from a different model family from the one you are watching.

Deter or incriminate

An agent that declines because it suspects a trap does no harm, but leaves no evidence. IAPS suggests gathering evidence while an agent’s intent is unknown, then switching to deterrence once it is clear.

▶ 012The reverse cuts both ways

Every trick here works on defenders’ agents too. Three examples from this research make the point.

Red teamers’ agents are trappable. Ureña’s backdoor ran on the operator’s machine, and two of the six tools exposed the operator’s AI token because they ran in the same container. If you point agents at targets, sandbox them and gate any binary they fetch. [URENA]

Refusal can blind a scanner. In Zenity’s skill-detonation work, its sandboxed agent refused to run obviously malicious skills until it was argued round. The speakers also noted that an LLM-based scanner can be made to refuse a scan. The context-bomb idea, aimed the other way, blinds a defender’s AI. [DETONATE]

Hidden markers are public text. Radware’s November preprint covers roughly 145 million GitHub items. It found 43 attacks aimed at other parties’ agents in issues, pull requests and comments, about one per 3.3 million items on those surfaces. Another 345 of its 2,281 findings on those surfaces were defensive, around 15%. The project’s own markers are public text too. An outsider can copy them, so check who wrote the instruction. [RADWARE]

▶ 013Where it breaks, and the hack-back line

Bear traps are not a silver bullet. Honeypots only catch paths you anticipated. IAPS adds that they suit diffuse threats poorly, such as subtle sabotage spread across many small actions, and its authors are less confident about much more capable agents. The GPT-5.5 maze run fits that warning. [IAPS]

Keep the scope of the evidence with the result:

  • Tracebit’s July study tested one AWS setup. A plain-canary comparison would help isolate what the refusal layer adds.
  • Zenity’s honeypot figures are counts of requests and observed activity on its decoy network. They tell you where to look, with no count of unique attackers or confirmed compromises.
  • BLA’s effectiveness figures and Tracebit’s studies are vendor or project research, not independently validated.
  • Ureña’s results are one researcher’s default-behaviour tests with five prompts. Different prompts or more retries could change the results.

Keep the trap on your side of the fence. Work within the systems you’re authorised to monitor, contain the decoy, and review what it collects. Ureña flags the legal risk of running code on an attacker’s machine. The recommendations here focus on observing activity in your own environment. [URENA]

▶ 014What to do on Monday

RoleAction
Blue team

Start with a plain honeytoken or a monitored decoy. Verify what actually fires the alert and who will act on it. If you trial a refusal layer, measure what it adds over the plain decoy.

Red team

Treat everything your agent reads as hostile. Run it in an isolated sandbox with no operator tokens, and gate any binary it fetches.

Builders

Give every agent its own identity so a trigger is attributable, log tamper-resistantly and make shutdown routine. Lock down LLM gateways and model servers, and rotate default keys.

Software vendors

Bind secrets to runtime state, and fail with plausible garbage, never a crash.

Researchers

Measure what the model did, not what its script did. Test decoys against the exact model, framework and tools.

The attacker sent an agent to hunt you. Don’t just block it. Give it something plausible to chase, watch what it touches, and follow the clues it leaves. Then play the card.

  1. [IAPS] Jan Wehner & Jam Kraprayoon, Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats (IAPS, October 2026). Policy report on detection, incrimination and deterrence.
  2. [URENA] Julio Ureña, Hacking Back AI Pentesting Agents (Plaintext Cybersecurity, October 2026). Controlled proof of concept. Five fixed prompts for the CLI tests.
  3. [MOQESH] Ureña, Moqesh. Open-source HoneyAI / TokenExhaust implementation.
  4. [TRACEBIT-CANARIES] Tracebit, AI Agents & Canaries (May 2026). Vendor benchmark for early detection and disclosure of possible deception.
  5. [TRACEBIT] Tracebit, Context Bombs: Stopping AI Attackers in Their Tracks (July 2026). Vendor benchmark. 152 scored runs across five models.
  6. [QUARKSLAB] Quarkslab, Defeating AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering (or at Least Trying To) (20 August 2026). Lab experiments.
  7. [BLA] qybaihe, BLA: Blind LLM Agents. Open-source project, MIT licence; self-reported benchmarks.
  8. [YOTAM] Yotam Perkal, Adversarial Deception in the Age of AI Attackers (AI Agent Security Summit, London, 8 October 2026). Speaker’s maze experiments.
  9. [ZENITY] Mike Takahashi (Zenity), Into the Wild: Hunting Real-World Attacks on AI Systems ([un]prompted II, 27 October 2026, Stage 2, 10:45). Honeypot traffic and case examples reported in the talk. See also Zenity’s overview of the honeypot network.
  10. [SHIBBOLETH] Dario Pasquini, Reworr, Giuseppe Ateniese, Manish Bhatt & Sergej Epp, Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks (November 2026). Research preprint with separate model and harness experiments.
  11. [RADWARE] Gabi Nakibly & Zvika Babo, Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? (21 November 2026). Research preprint covering roughly 145 million GitHub items.
  12. [DETONATE] Tamir Ishay Sharbat & Joao Donato (Zenity), Promptware EOD: Skillful Agent Detonation ([un]prompted II, 27 October 2026, Stage 2, 12:00). Conference talk on testing suspicious agent skills in containment.
  13. [STRAND] Strand et al., Offensive Countermeasures: The Art of Active Defense (Black Hills Information Security). Origin of the annoyance, attribution, attack model.
  14. [ACTIVE] Dark Reading, How I Learned To Love Active Defense. Defines the “triple A” categories.
  15. [ADHD] Dark Reading, Free ‘Active Defense’ Tools Emerge. Strand on staying short of hacking back.
  16. [ENISA] ENISA, Information Operations: Active Defence and Offensive Countermeasures. Uses the term for counter-attack.
